attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create and export a new sprite kind inside the SpriteKind namespace at the top of the editor?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡 The ninja can also modify or create their own images to serve as the pizza toppings.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by declaring a new sprite kind and adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Notice there is already code in the editor; there are image variables under the comment // image set up. 


Underneath this starter code, add comments with these descriptions to the project: function set up, game set up, function calls. Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.


Above // image set up, add the comment // sprite kind set up. Underneath, access the SpriteKind namespace by typing the keyword namespace then SpriteKind and a pair of curly brackets { }


Inside the curly brackets, type the keyword export then use let and the name of the new sprite kind that will be used for the pizza topping sprites, Topping, an assignment operator, and the SpriteKind.create() function to create a new sprite kind within the namespace.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an equality operator inside the parentheses of the if condition to check if the value of the question variable is equal to “y”?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What topping might you ask the user if they want on their pizza?

❓ What might happen if the user answers “y” to the question?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure that the ninja has used a topping name from one of the image variables already created in the code and that they’ve included “y” in their string message.
steps.instructions:
Set a background image and ask for user input on the pizza toppings!


Open Scene and drag [set background image to (img)] under // game set up. Replace img `` with the name of the pizza image variable from the starter code.


Declare a new variable called question underneath // function set up. Open Game and drag [ask for string (message)] to the right side of the assignment operator. Replace null with a string that asks the user if they want one of the topping options, using “y” to confirm. Update the answerLength parameter to 1


Open Logic and drag [if] underneath the variable code. Inside the parentheses of the if condition, use an equality operator to check if the value of the question variable is equal to “y”.


Click ▶ to see the question appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the run condition so that the loop continues to run as long as the counter variable is less than randomNum ?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many times will the for loop run?

❓ What will happen if the user responds “y” to the question?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the for loop will continue to run while the counter variable is less than the value of the randomNum variable. This will cause a different number of topping sprites to be created and placed each time.

💡 If the user responds “y” to the question, a random number of Topping sprites will be placed on the pizza. Encourage the ninja to test out the project to make sure that the range of possible positions in the setPosition code places the Topping sprites on the pizza.
steps.instructions:
Use a for loop to create a random number of toppings on the pizza.


Inside the curly brackets of the if conditional, declare a new variable called randomNum. Use randint to assign it a random value between 4 and 7


Open Loops and drag [for] underneath the variable code, inside the conditional. Update the run condition to i < randomNum so the loop will run the number of times determined by randomNum.


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop. Update the sprite name, replace img`...` with one of the topping image variables, and change the sprite kind to Topping. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] under sprites.create. Update the sprite name, then use randint to set the Topping sprites’ x and y-positions so they only appear on top of the pizza in the background image.


Click ▶ to see a random number of toppings appear on top of the pizza!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the push function on the empty string array inside the if conditional so that the topping is added to the array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What types of elements can be stored in the pizzaToppings array?

❓ Why might the topping name be pushed to the pizzaToppings array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has included a colon :, the type string, and a pair of brackets [ ] before the assignment operator in the pizzaToppings array declaration. Point out to the ninja that the string type appears in blue and has a lowercase s.

💡 Explain to the ninja that each time the user says “y” to a topping, its name (as a string value) will be pushed to the end of the pizzaToppings array. These elements will be able to be referenced later in the project.
steps.instructions:
Create an empty array to store the user-selected toppings!


Underneath the image variable code, use the keyword let to declare an empty array called pizzaToppings. Since pizzaToppings will contain strings, use : string[] after the array name. Then, type an assignment operator and a second pair of brackets [ ] 


Store the selected toppings in the array by adding code inside the curly brackets { } of the if conditional, under the for loop. Type the name of the array and a dot operator . then select push from the code completion tool and type a pair of parentheses ( ). Inside the parentheses, type the name of the topping from the question as a string.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare the function’s string and image parameters, then move the question variable and if conditional code inside the function definition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is defining a new function in JavaScript similar and different to defining a function in the blocks editor?

❓ What are some functions that you have already used in the JavaScript editor?

❓ How is setting the type of a function parameter similar to setting the type in an empty array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that functions enable a project to reuse a chunk of code more easily. By using a function, the code is simplified, more organized, and easier to read.

💡 In the blocks editor, the ninja created a function by dragging out a function definition container. In the JavaScript editor, a function can be created by dragging out function doSomething] from the menu. In the JavaScript editor, parameters are typed inside of the function’s parentheses and code is added inside of the curly brackets.
steps.instructions:
Define a function that asks the user if they’d like different toppings!


Click Advanced then open Functions and drag [function doSomething] under // function set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


function doSomething() {...}

Replace doSomething with a new function name: makePizza


Inside the parentheses, declare 2 parameters: a string and an Image. First, type the name of the parameter, such as toppingName, then a colon : to set the type of the parameter it will be: string. Add a comma, then declare an Image parameter called toppingImage. The code may look like: 


function makePizza(toppingName:string, toppingImage: Image)

Cut (Ctrl + X) the question variable and if conditional code, then paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the function’s curly brackets.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the toppingName and toppingImage parameters in the code inside the makePizza function definition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How are the function’s parameters used to change what happens when the function is called?

❓ What topping image will appear on the screen when the function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the function needs to be called in order for its code to run. This will happen in the next step.

💡 Explain to the ninja that when a function is called, values will be submitted to set the parameters. In this example, the values will update the strings in the askForString and push code, and the image in the sprites.create code.
steps.instructions:
Add the function’s parameters to the code inside the function so it can be used for different toppings!


In the askForString function, update the topping name string with toppingName, using + signs to concatenate the parameter value with the rest of the question.


In the sprites.create code, replace the image variable name with the parameter toppingImage.


In the push code, replace the string inside the parentheses with the parameter toppingName.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the makePizza function 4 times, passing different string and image arguments each time?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is calling a function in the JavaScript editor similar and different to calling a function in the blocks editor?

❓ How do the values in the function calls change the code that runs in the function definition?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that a function needs to be defined then called separately, in order for its code to run.

💡 In the blocks editor, the ninja called a function by dragging out a [call function] block. In the JavaScript editor, a function can be called by typing the function name, followed by a pair of parentheses. Arguments that are of the same type as the parameters declared in the function definition, should be typed inside of the parentheses, separated by commas. 

💡 Explain to the ninja that the arguments inside the parentheses of each function call will be passed to the parameters inside the function definition code. The string and image values must match so that the name that appears in the question matches the image placed on the pizza.
steps.instructions:
Call the function to ask the user which toppings they’d like on their pizza! 


Under // function calls, type the name of the makePizza function followed by a pair of parentheses ( ). Inside the parentheses, pass 2 arguments to the function by typing the string name of the topping, a comma, then the image variable name. The code may look like: 

makePizza(“pepperoni”, pepperoni)

Call the function 3 more times, replacing the 2 arguments inside the parentheses with the 3 other topping options. 


Click ▶ to see the program ask the user about all 4 topping options!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update both the kind and otherKind parameters to Topping in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the kind and otherKind parameters both be set to Topping in the onOverlap event?

❓ What will happen if 2 Topping sprites overlap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In order for all of the Topping sprites to be visible on the pizza, code should be added to change the position of Topping sprites on overlap with each other. Encourage the ninja to test out the project to see the Topping sprites move if they are overlapping.
steps.instructions:
Move the Topping sprites’ positions so they do not overlap!


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath the function call code. Change the kind and otherKind parameters both to Topping. 


Copy (Ctrl + C) the setPosition code from the makePizza function definition, then paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the onOverlap event. Use sprite from the onOverlap event as the sprite name.


Click ▶ to see the Topping sprites change position if they are overlapping another Topping sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type “ + ” inside the join function so that each element from the array will be joined with a + in between each topping name?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What should be displayed when the second dialog box appears?

❓ What symbol is placed between each value in the pizzaToppings array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that each time the user responded “y” to the question, that topping name was added to the pizzaToppings array. Once all of the toppings have been added, the project can report back to the user what their order was, displaying all of the elements in the pizzaToppings array.

💡 Remind the ninja that the join function joins all the elements of an array into a single string value. The string separator parameter sets what will be placed between each value. In this case, a plus sign + will be placed between each value in the pizzaToppings array. Remind the Ninja to add spaces on either side of the + inside the quotation marks, and to test the project to ensure the text syntax appears correctly.
steps.instructions:
Use dialog boxes, pause, and sounds to report what pizza toppings the user ordered!


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath the onOverlap event. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares a string that introduces the user’s order. 


Copy (Ctrl + C) the code from the first showLongText, then paste (Ctrl + V) it on the line below. Replace the string with pizzaToppings, then type a dot operator and select join from the code completion tool. After join, type a pair of parentheses with “ + ” inside. This will set the string separator parameter to join each value from the array with a + in between each topping name. 


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] below the showLongText code. Set the parameter so that the project pauses briefly after the toppings have been listed.


Open Music and drag [play (toPlay) (playbackMode)] below the pause code, then use the dot operator to select an appropriate sound for the reveal of the pizza.


Click ▶ to see the list of toppings appear after the user gives the order!

steps.hints: ❓ What title or directions would help users understand how the game works?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What title or directions might tell the user what the project is about or how to play? 

❓ How long should the project pause before asking the user a question?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a splash screen and a pause before the start of the project!


Open Game and drag [splash (title)] underneath the setBackgroundImage code in // game set up. Update the title parameters, so that a splash screen shares directions or a title of the project with the user.


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] below the splash code. Update the parameter, so that the project pauses briefly on the empty pizza crust before asking the user for their order.


Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.title: Pizza Party
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses functions to create a pizza based on user input.

validationItems.text: Declare a new Topping sprite kind.
Set a pizza background image and ask the user for a string.
Use a conditional statement and a for loop to create a random number of toppings.
Create an empty pizzaToppings string array to store the user selected toppings.
Create a makePizza function with string and Image parameters that asks the user if they want different toppings.
Call the makePizza function 4 times, once for each topping option.
Reposition a Topping sprite if it overlaps with another Topping sprite.
Use dialog boxes and the join function to share the user’s pizza order.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about functions. Functions can be used to name a unique chunk of code that can be easily reused in a project. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Function Junction
badges.description: Create and call functions that use different parameter types in JavaScript.

badges.title: Functional Thinking
badges.description: Create a new function, with or without parameters, in JavaScript.

badges.title: Calling All Functions
badges.description: Call a function, with or without parameters, in JavaScript.

badges.title: Time for a Change
badges.description: Change the border color of the countdown timer.

badges.title: Feeling Shifty
badges.description: Use the shift function to remove and return the first value in an array.

badges.title: Read the Manual
badges.description: Use a block comment to document a function.

badges.title: Free Fallin’
badges.description: Set the acceleration of a sprite to simulate gravity.
